lines.caption: Every Friday, Wanjiru's chama puts in a thousand shillings each. This week, it's her turn.
But one treasurer collects it all, in cash or on one phone, and the whole group has to trust them.
8.7 million Kenyans save in groups like this.
This is Zamu. Your chama, paid straight to M-Pesa.
This is the real app, inside Nimiq Pay on a phone. Open it from Mini Apps.
Sign in by signing a message with your own Nimiq key. Nobody types a password.
Start a chama: the share, how often, how many, and the M-Pesa number your turn is paid to.
Ask for less than fifteen shillings, and Zamu says so before anything is saved.
Then share the invite code, or the QR code, with your group.
When everyone has joined, each member signs the agreement with their own Nimiq key.
Each round, members tap Pay. Nimiq Pay swaps their NIM or USDT to Lightning, and a payout partner turns it into exact shillings in Wanjiru's M-Pesa.
A share only turns green when the M-Pesa receipt comes back, and the whole group can open it.
If Nimiq Pay can't tell whether a payment went out, Zamu never lets you pay twice. It checks, and waits.
And anyone who stops paying loses their turn until they catch up.
Under the hood, Nimiq Pay signs and pays. Zamu checks every invoice: Bitcoin mainnet, the exact amount, the right phone, still valid. A job on AWS keeps checking until the receipt arrives.
On a live quote today, the payout leg cost one percent over the partner's own rate.
Real payouts are next, and every number will come from our proof script.
Shares land in M-Pesa, not a group wallet. Paid means a receipt. Everyone signs with Nimiq. No treasurer holds the pot.
Friday again. Wanjiru's phone buzzes: five thousand shillings, and a receipt for every share.
Zamu. Open it in Nimiq Pay.
